1:
This was no border raid, and Ellicott measures it. The muster was a great effort, as Josephus remarks, nothing like the incursions frequent through Saul's reign, and no such army had been gathered since the Philistine defeat in the valley of Elah. What strikes him is the geography: the enemy is in the heart of the land, no longer contesting the familiar marches, strong enough to challenge a battle on the plain of Esdraelon north of Ephraim and Issachar. He reconstructs the march along the sea-border of Canaan, gathering forces as it went, then turning inland by the valley of Jezreel to a position near Shunem. Clarke supplies a conjecture of Isaac Newton's for the new strength, that the armies had been swelled by men whom Amasis drove out of Egypt, and adds that Samuel's death and David's disgrace were motives to a fresh war from which the Philistines had everything to hope. Henry answers from the other side: had Israel not forsaken God there would have been no Philistines left to molest them.

David's position is judged severely by two and gently by one. Keil and Delitzsch see the danger of his flight into Philistia, and still more of the artifice by which he had deceived Achish, coming home to him now that he was summoned into the Philistine army against his own people and could not refuse; but they plead that he had taken refuge there only in the last extremity and had done the rest to save his life, and that the covenant God helped him out and soon ended his persecution by Saul's death. Ellicott allows no such mitigation. Want of faith and patience had driven him to the hereditary foes of his people, and the sixteen months in Philistia succeeded only in establishing him as a free-lance captain, stained with bloodshed and cruelty, his life one of duplicity and falsehood.

Ellicott traces the consequences a long way out. The nation sustained a crushing defeat which David narrowly escaped having to witness, if not to assist; his recognition as king was put off nearly seven years, in which a civil war hindered the country's prosperity; and in that time of division the seeds were laid of the later separation of Judah from the northern tribes, which came about in his grandson's reign. Henry fixes on the dilemma of the moment: to promise help and then stand neuter or go over to Israel would be treachery, while to fight against Israel would be a great sin, so that it seemed impossible to get out with a clear conscience; and he judges the evasive answer, meant to gain time, not consistent with the character of an Israelite indeed.

The answer itself is read three ways. Clarke calls it equivocal and says only David's later conduct could settle which way it pointed, and that Achish took it in the Philistines' favour; Wesley notes simply that he speaks ambiguously, as before. Henry reconstructs the mental reservation, that David would consider in what post he might best serve if allowed to choose it, keeping himself free of a promise while leaving its expectation standing. Gill prefers a third reading over both: that David was quite undetermined and at a loss, hoping God in his providence would extricate him and show him what to do, as in the event he did. On the offer, Clarke and Henry both take the keeping of the king's head to mean captain of the life-guards, Henry adding protector or prime minister of state. Ellicott thinks Achish was simply won, like so many others, by the loveable character of the son of Jesse, and would see no ambiguity at all; the king's blind confidence was not shared by the Philistine lords, whose jealousy of the distinguished stranger opened their eyes, and they may have hoped to set their friend on Saul's throne as a vassal king.
3:
Two facts already on record are repeated here, and each asks why. Gill answers that Samuel's death accounts both for the Philistines renewing the war and for Saul's resorting to a witch to raise the man who was dead. Clarke puts the consequence in one clause, that there was no longer a public accredited prophet to consult. Ellicott reconstructs the compiler's purpose: Samuel, whom Saul was so anxious to see, was dead and buried, and the possessors of familiar spirits whose aid he was about to invoke had long since been put out of the land by his own order. He adds that the versions dropped the repetition, not seeing why it was there.

The two classes of practitioner are examined. Ellicott admits the first word has never been explained with certainty, though scholars connect it with a root meaning to be hollow, so that it denotes a hollow thing or bag and thence one who speaks in a hollow voice; what it appears to mean is the ventriloquist's distended belly, and it is used both of the practitioner and of the spirit supposed to speak from within. The second is literally the wise people, a name he thinks given in irony to dealers in forbidden arts. The Mosaic command was clear and decisive, and Saul in his early zeal put it in force after it had long lain in abeyance. Henry canvasses when: some place the edict early in the reign, under Samuel's influence, others make it recent, since it is later spoken of as a late decree. He offers a motive fitting the later date, that a man troubled with an evil spirit might suspect he was bewitched and cut off all who had familiar spirits for that reason, and generalises it, since many seem zealous against sin when hurt by it who have no dislike of sin as sin. The enforcement he still calls commendable, noting the irony that a man who would drive the devil out of his kingdom harboured him in his own heart, and was about to consult the very people he had tried to root out.

The ground matters, because the two camps were in sight of each other. Keil and Delitzsch put Gilboa on the north-eastern edge of the plain of Jezreel, falling from about twelve hundred and fifty feet into the Jordan valley, with Shunem hardly two hours off, so that the Philistine camp could be seen from the Israelite one. Ellicott makes the range white chalk and rather higher, and places the Philistines on the slope opposite, parted from Saul by the deep valley, their whole army plainly visible from his high ground.

On the fear they agree, and agree that the numbers are not the real cause. Keil and Delitzsch point out that Saul had beaten the Philistines more than once, so his terror can hardly be put down to anything but the feeling that God had forsaken him, which overwhelmed him suddenly. Clarke lists three grounds, the superiority of the enemy, the state of his own army, and above all his own state towards God. Ellicott grants the ranks were more numerous than Saul expected, but locates the trembling in the same consciousness, and sets the scene: the forsaken king on the white chalk hill, looking at the lines of tents and wondering whether his old friend was among them in the division of Gath. Wesley reduces it to a condition, that had he kept close to God he need not have feared all the armies of the Philistines. Henry fills in what a guilty conscience supplied, his sins set in order before his eyes, the spared blood of the Amalekites and the spilt blood of the priests, so that a man who had provoked God to forsake him trembled at the shaking of a leaf.
6:
Three channels were open and all were silent. Clarke numbers them: a dream begged of God in prayer; the oracular reply given to the high priest wearing the ephod with the Urim and Thummim, though how it was communicated is not well known; and the prophets, asked by the enquirer to consult the Lord and report. He adds that the prophets available then could only have been those in the schools Samuel founded at Naioth and Gibeah, the only successors of Samuel we know of. Gill doubts whether the enquiry deserved the name, not being made truly or heartily nor persisted in, so that, as Kimchi observes, it was as if none had been made, especially once the man went on to enquire of one that had a familiar spirit. Keil and Delitzsch put the failure down to what Saul did next: instead of recognising the silence and searching his heart, he set about getting a revelation of the future by ungodly means.

Ellicott asks what the others do not: how the enquiry was made at all. Since the massacre at Nob, the priest who held the ephod and breastplate was in David's camp, and we hear of a solemn use of them there. His answer, credited to eminent scholars, is that Saul moved the sanctuary from desecrated Nob to Gibeon, where the Tabernacle stands in the first year of David's reign with Zadok as high priest, probably put there by Saul; which would also explain the two high priests under David, Zadok over the Tabernacle and Abiathar, who had fled from Nob with the ephod. It was this Zadok, Ellicott assumes, who enquired for Saul, perhaps by an ephod made in imitation of the real breastplate; no response was received, and prophets of Samuel's school, likely present too, received no message either.

The turn to the witch reads as collapse, not calculation. Ellicott describes the last spark of a zeal once shown even to excess vanishing, or rather turning, as zeal must when it swerves from the moral principle that alone can guide it, into wild and desperate superstition, so that the spirits he had driven out in a fit of righteous indignation became his only resource. Henry lays two charges: contempt of the God of Israel, as though any creature could help a man God has left, and self-contradiction, since the heinousness of witchcraft was what the edict assumed. He generalises it, that men inveigh severely against the sins they are in no temptation to and are afterwards overcome by them, and imagines the answer Saul would have given had anyone predicted this while he destroyed the witches: what, is thy servant a dog?

What Saul asked for is given its proper name. Keil and Delitzsch render it the mistress of a conjuring spirit, the spirit by which the dead were called up to be questioned about the future, and Clarke the mistress of the Pythonic spirit, whom she could invoke at pleasure. Wesley puts it more bluntly: one that converses with the devil or with dead men's ghosts. On the place, Keil and Delitzsch note that Endor still exists under its old name on the northern shoulder of the Little Hermon, and both they and Clarke put it ten miles from the camp. Ellicott quotes Conder for what it looks like, a village of mud-huts with prickly-pear hedges east of Nain, and for what the journey cost, since to reach it the king had to pass the hostile camp and would have crept round the eastern shoulder of the hill under cover of the ground. He records the tradition that the companions were Abner and Amasa, and the woman Abner's mother, which if true would explain her escape. Gill notes that Saul spoke only to servants he could trust, and Henry that they proved too officious, naming one at Endor who had escaped his own edict.
8:
The disguise is given four motives. Gill has Saul laying aside royal or military dress for a common soldier's, so that he should be unknown to the woman and able to leave his army unremarked, nobody knowing that he had gone or where. Clarke and Wesley add the practical fear, that the woman, if she knew him, would be terrified and refuse her art; Wesley adds shame at being thought guilty of it. Ellicott notices that the darkness served twice over, hiding the king from the witch and giving him a better chance of slipping past the Philistine army between him and Endor. Henry reads it as degradation: never did Saul look so mean as when he went sneaking to a sorry witch to know his fortune, and the costume was to keep his own people from abhorring him as much as to keep the woman from refusing. Such is the power of natural conscience, he says, that even those who do evil blush to do it.

The request gets more attention from Ellicott than from anyone else. Keil and Delitzsch gloss it as divining through necromancy, and suppose that prophesying this way was done by calling a departed spirit up from Sheol and getting disclosures about one's own fate through it. Ellicott quotes that and observes that no other commentator here touches the matter, while Keil leaves undecided whether the thing named was a spirit kept at the sorceress's service or the soul of someone already dead. His own account is that the sorcerer possessed, or was supposed to possess, a familiar, through whose aid a departed spirit was compelled or induced to revisit the world and submit to questioning; and the word for divining, he notes, is of Syriac origin, as most such words are.

Ellicott puts the practice in a longer frame. If the power existed at all, Israel learned it from the original inhabitants of Canaan, and these arts have fascinated men in every age, so that even now the dead are invoked and questioned as in Saul's. On the phrase about bringing up, he notes that the popular idea always placed the dead beneath the ground as heaven was placed above, and that the Church has taken the language into her creeds. Keil and Delitzsch defend the idiom rather than apologise for it: with modes of thought so bound up with time and space, there is no other way to represent the contrast between blessedness with God and the shade-life in death.

The objection and the oath are weighed against each other. Keil and Delitzsch see her genuinely caught, since the man who had expelled the necromancers might be an informer come to spy her out and have her executed under the law. Ellicott agrees the law was still in force and such women had often been hunted down by informers, though the tradition making her Abner's mother would rule out that particular fear; he suggests another motive, that enhancing her peril might extort a larger present. Henry finds providence in the timing, that Saul should be told his own edict to his face at the moment he was breaking it, and measures her fear exactly: alive to the danger from Saul's law, not at all apprehensive of God's, she feared a snare laid for her life more than one laid for her soul. Gill marvels that a man about such a work could take the name of the Lord into his mouth and swear so solemnly, which must have reminded him of an omniscience nothing is hidden from; Keil and Delitzsch call the oath a measure of how hardened he was. Henry adds the absurdity, that a king bound by divine command to punish her swore as though his oath could release him, and promised what he could not perform, since a man who could not secure himself could hardly secure her.
11:
What the woman believed she was offering is set out carefully. Gill notes that such practitioners professed to bring up any of the dead whom the enquirer should name, and Clarke holds that she meant no more than having her familiar personify whoever was asked for, since by the professed rules of the art that is all such persons pretend to, having no power at all over human souls. Even granting an art founded on true principles, he says, the most it could do is bring up the familiar, make him assume the form and character of a particular person, and report such notices of the future as he can collect; and even where authenticity is allowed this is often vague and uncertain, since fallen spirits do not abound in knowledge. He presses further than the verse requires: Satan himself is cunning and insidious rather than wise, and we generally credit him with far more wisdom than he has.

Why Samuel was asked for draws out the pathos. Henry observes that while Samuel lived at Ramah, close to Gibeah, we never read of Saul consulting him in any difficulty, having slighted and perhaps hated him as a man in David's interest; now that he is dead the cry is for Samuel again, and many who despise God's ministers while they live would be glad of them once they are gone. Ellicott describes a man who felt himself forsaken of God and whose mind turned nevertheless to the friend and guide of his youth, from whom he had been hopelessly estranged long before that friend died, and quotes Trench for the thing itself: something unutterably pathetic in the yearning of the dis-anointed king, in his utter desolation, to exchange words once more with the counsellor of his youth, and if he must hear his doom, to hear it from no other lips. Wesley puts it as expectation rather than longing: Saul had known Samuel's kindness before and looked for it now.

What the narrative does not say is itself noticed. Henry calls it a seeming chasm, since Saul says bring me up Samuel and the next words are that the woman saw Samuel, with nothing between about spells or charms or how it was performed; and he reads the silence as deliberate, forbidding any coveting to know the depths of Satan, since it has been said of some confessors' books that their descriptions of sin taught men to commit it, whereas scripture conceals sinful art so that we may be simple concerning evil. Gill says the same, that the methods are withheld to check curiosity and prevent imitation, and mentions without favouring the view that the apparition came before she used any arts.

The cry settles something for three of them. Keil and Delitzsch argue from it that she saw an apparition she had not anticipated, so that she either merely pretended to the power or, if her craft had some demoniacal background, met with something essentially unlike anything she had produced before, which filled her with alarm; and they note that recognising Saul the moment Samuel appeared tells against calling the whole thing trickery. Clarke is blunter: Samuel did appear, and was raised neither by the devil's power nor by the woman's incantations, since her familiar did not come and her confused description shows her surprised by what she had not expected. Wesley says the words are express, that she saw Samuel instead of the spirit she looked for, God so ordering it for his own glory. On how she knew her visitor, Ellicott canvasses three answers: Ewald's, that the shade rose with gestures of threat it could only have used against Saul; Keil's, that she had fallen into a clairvoyant state; and Josephus's, that Samuel revealed the king's presence by speaking to him as Saul. Ellicott prefers the last, and thinks some word not reported here betrayed him.
13:
The plural noun the woman uses is the chapter's first crux. Keil and Delitzsch rule out most of the options: it signifies neither gods nor God, nor an angel or ghost, but a celestial, super-terrestrial being. Clarke points out that the word is used of the Supreme Being throughout the Bible, that every version but one renders it plural as the English does, and that the exception has an angel of the Lord ascending from the earth; the sight alarmed the woman, who could not recognise her familiar in it. Ellicott prefers the singular sense, since the best modern scholars reason from Saul's following question about the form that one God-like figure is meant, majestic and august; yet antiquity leaned the other way, a Talmud passage speaking of two spirit forms. Wesley takes the plural for a Hebrew idiom used of one person, or else for the language of the heathen, and Henry hears the heathen in it too, with their infernal deities, and cannot resist the aside: poor gods that ascend out of the earth.

The mantle settles the identification, and raises a question of its own. Keil and Delitzsch identify it as the prophet's mantle Samuel wore in life, from which Saul knew who had come and fell on his face in reverence; that he does not appear to have seen the apparition himself proves nothing against its reality, since it needs an opened eye to see a departed spirit. Clarke infers a sequence instead, the old man in the mantle being a second apparition, the earlier angelic one having prepared the way, the whole arranged to show the woman that her art had not prevailed and that what happened was independent of her incantations. Ellicott asks how a spirit could bear the semblance of an old man and be clothed at all, and answers out of Maimonides, who observes that scripture uses such language of the Holy One himself, the finger of God and a garment white as snow, all of it belonging to an apparition of prophecy; and out of Wordsworth, that if Samuel's spirit was to be recognised by human eyes it could only be by means visible to human sense, as Moses was presented at the Transfiguration in a garb that let the disciples know him.

Whether it was Samuel at all divides them, and Henry stands alone. Had the body been wanted, he argues, the witch would have been taken to Ramah where the sepulchre was; the design was on the soul, and God permitted the devil to put on Samuel's shape, so that men who would not receive the love of the truth should be given up to strong delusion. The ascent out of the earth itself betrays the imposture, he thinks, since the spirit of a man, much more of a good man, goes upward; and the devil's personating him is no marvel in one who can transform himself into an angel of light. Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch hold the contrary, that Samuel did appear and was raised neither by the woman nor by the devil, and Wesley puts the consequence as a dilemma: if it was not Samuel but another spirit in his shape, then it is not true that Saul perceived it was Samuel. On the obeisance Henry allows two motives, reverence to a man he could not see, or a posture for catching the soft muttering voice he expected, since those who had familiar spirits peeped and muttered — and he draws the sting, that the man who would not stoop to the word of God stooped to this. Ellicott thinks the king probably saw the form at that moment, though the wording leaves open whether the homage followed only the woman's description; Gill explains why he may have seen nothing, the woman standing between him and the apparition.
15:
The opening reproach is evidence to some and neutral to others. Gill treats it as decisive: a soul at rest in Abraham's bosom is beyond the power of men or devils to disquiet, and the real prophet would have spoken of coming down rather than of being brought up, still less conceded that a witch and the devil had fetched him. Henry argues the same from bishop Patrick, that witches cannot disturb the rest of good men at pleasure, and that Samuel would never have allowed such power to magical arts; to Saul, though, the complaint was a shrewd device, drawing veneration and fixing in him an opinion of divination's power. Keil and Delitzsch read only what the words say, citing Isaiah 14:9: Samuel had been disturbed from his rest, and whether by the woman's arts or by a miracle of God is left undecided. Ellicott reports a commentator who infers that the incantation itself produced the result, and sides against him: the words assert the disturbance and ask its reason without settling what power effected it. Clarke notes the reproach is aimed at Saul, not the woman, whose operations had no influence and seem not to have begun before the way was prepared.

What Saul says, and what he omits, draws comment of its own. Henry notes that the king never complained of God's withdrawing until trouble came, and that a man who had not sought God in prosperity thought it hard to go unanswered in adversity; the complaint owns no righteousness in the stroke but flies out against God, expecting a servant of God to befriend the man God frowns on and a dead prophet to outdo living ones. His summary is that advice sought otherwise than from God is sought from the devil, capped with the tag about moving hell when heaven will not bend. A preacher quoted by Ellicott hears the same in the cry — pathos and a weird awesomeness, but no confession of sin and no plea for mercy, only the ambition to preserve himself — and Ellicott sets beside it Shakespeare's Richard III before Bosworth and Macbeth at Dunsinane, heavy with shapeless dread. Wesley's regret is shorter: happy had he called Samuel sooner, or rather the God of Samuel, destruction being now at hand. On the unmentioned breastplate oracle, Keil and Delitzsch blame the brevity of the narrative, while Ellicott prefers an answer from the Talmud: it was no longer in Saul's kingdom, having been worn by the high priest he had murdered, and shame over Nob stopped the word in his throat.

The answer's first move refuses the question. Gill has the speaker reasoning in language that might pass for the prophet's own, though he betrays himself at points; the force of the retort is that a prophet of the Lord can say nothing but what comes from the Lord. Clarke puts it as a question: was he ever accustomed to give answers not dictated by God, whose counsel alone he communicates? Ellicott restates it plainly — if Jehovah has left you, why consult his servant? — then pauses over the word rendered enemy, which occurs only once elsewhere and has been taken for an Aramaic form, though this book is pure classical Hebrew and shows no other such forms; a slight slip of the copyist in its first letter would account for it, and the Greek and Latin versions evidently read something else, giving "and is with thy neighbours." Henry finds the reply cold comfort, calculated to drive the man to despair and self-murder. The true Samuel, asked what to do, would have said repent, make peace with God and recall David, and would have held out mercy; this speaker calls the case hopeless, dealing with Saul as with Judas, first a tempter and then a tormentor, and asking how he could befriend one whose God had turned enemy.
17:
The two charges are old ones, and the first of them carries a textual question. Gill reads the opening clause as spoken about David, Saul's supposed enemy. Clarke takes it as spoken about Saul and argues the pronoun should be second person, citing the Latin and Greek, five of Kennicott's and De Rossi's manuscripts, and both Venice Bibles of 1518; of the claim to divine authority he says there was no illusion here, and none but Samuel could have said it. Ellicott prefers the marginal rendering, that the Lord has performed this for himself, and calls the versions' second person a needless alteration of the text. Bishop Wordsworth, quoted by Ellicott against the view that the shade was an evil spirit, reasons that no evil spirit would have wished to help David to the throne, or spoken so solemnly of the punishment due to rebellion. The second charge reaches back to Amalek, which Gill ties to the disobedience at Gilgal and the first threat against the kingdom. Henry hears both as calculated cruelty: the anointing of David touched the string that sounded most unpleasant in Saul's ear, nothing said to reconcile them and everything to widen the breach, while the old sin, once palliated when repentance was the aim, is now aggravated to make him despair of mercy.

The sentence itself Ellicott breaks into three judgments: the utter defeat of the army, the violent death of the king and his sons, and the sacking of the camp that would follow the rout and multiply its horrors. He notes that the word rendered host is better taken as camp, and cites the observation that the people's overthrow was itself part of Saul's misery, since he saw them ruined with him through his own sin. On the word rendered to-morrow, Ellicott holds it need not mean the next day but some near future time, where Henry, reckoning that the night was already past midnight, sees no reason not to take it strictly of the day then beginning. Henry also catches the device in the message's form: to be believed the speaker had to claim that God spoke by him, and the devil knows how to speak with an air of religion — which those who defend spells on the ground that they find nothing bad in them might consider, since nothing could be better said than this, or said to worse purpose.

The promise of company in death is the hardest phrase, and nobody reads it as damnation. Ellicott denies that Samuel pronounces a final sentence, having no mission to do so, and takes the words as mild and applicable to anyone: you shall be as I am, no longer among the living. He supports this from Dives and Lazarus, who are in one abode of departed spirits and can see and speak across the gulf fixed between them; from Bishop Wordsworth, that to have said you shall be among the damned would have crushed and hardened the man, whereas the gentler word exhorted him to repentance while life and the open door remained; and from St. Augustine, that the likeness is of condition in death, not equality in bliss. Clarke asks whether paradise is meant, concludes the words say no more than that they should all die, yet quotes with approval a stanza he credits to the Rev. C. Wesley that hopes otherwise, and adds that Saul had committed the sin visited with a violent death while mercy was still extended to the soul. Wesley quotes the same stanza in a slightly different form, allowing the same minimal sense. Gill and Henry, holding the speaker a foul spirit, point out that the prediction needed no revelation: the Philistine armies were numerous, Israel's weak, the king dispirited and God withdrawn, so a shrewd guess would serve — and an evil spirit foretold Ahab's fall at Ramoth-Gilead and helped bring it about.
20:
The collapse is described with some care. Gill has him fall at his full length at once, as though thunderstruck or run through; Clarke reads the Hebrew as falling with the fullness of his own stature, a man so overwhelmed that he swooned where he stood. Ellicott reconstructs the posture it interrupted, the king having knelt until then in the reverence he assumed on recognising the prophet, and adds the physical causes: a long fast and the fatigue of the rough night walk from Mount Gilboa to En-dor. Henry presses the fast further. Saul had eaten nothing that day or night, coming fasting from the camp and continuing so, not for want of food but for want of appetite — the fear of the Philistines had taken it away, or else the struggle with his own conscience once he had entertained the thought of consulting a witch made him nauseate even necessary food. That emptiness left him an easy prey when the fresh terror came on him like an armed man. Wesley's phrase is that he fell as though the Philistine archers had already hit him, with no strength left to bear up against such tidings.

What the collapse shows about the man divides two readings. Henry's is severe and consistent: Saul asked to be told what he should do and was told only what he had not done and what would be done to him, which is the disappointment awaiting anyone who looks for counsel outside God's own institutions. He had had enough of consulting witches and found them miserable comforters, for when God speaks terror in his word he opens a door of hope to the penitent, whereas those who apply at the gates of hell for succour must expect darkness with no glimpse of light. His verdict on the night is that the king was terrified to despair and yet never humbled — no confession, no sacrifice, no supplication — and that God sets up a few such beacons to warn men against stifling their convictions. Wesley will not go that far. He takes it as beyond doubt that all Saul's past sins were brought to his remembrance, and asks what authority any man has to affirm he felt no contrition at all, merely because the Holy Ghost did not see fit to record it.

Where the woman had been standing is a small question answered three ways. Gill and Wesley both have her withdraw to another room once she had brought the king and the apparition together, so that they might converse the more freely, and come back when she heard him fall. Clarke has her terrified at the prophet's first appearance and withdrawn to some distance, leaving Saul alone, until after a short time she returned, found him sore troubled, and offered the help that common humanity dictated. Keil and Delitzsch deny that the phrase requires an adjoining room at all; she stood at some distance and came up when he had fallen. Her motive divides them again. Ellicott finds a woman's pity in a grievous sinner, and argues from her behaviour against the theory that she hated Saul and faked the voice by ventriloquism: she was frightened by the apparition herself, and then saddened by the effect of its words on the king. Henry allows her very little, suspecting that she feared being punished as a traitor if he sickened or died in her house, having already escaped punishment as a witch, and remarking what a condition the king had brought himself to when he needed so wretched a comforter. Her plea, as Henry and Keil and Delitzsch both report it, is an exchange: she obeyed his voice at the risk of her life, so let him now hearken to her voice for the relief of his, and take enough to put strength in him for the road back.
22:
Gill states the woman's argument as an exchange: she had listened at the risk of her life, so he might listen where his own was to be preserved. The refusal is read two ways. Gill allows that the king may have been choosing famine over the Philistine sword, but thinks it likelier he could not eat, his stomach loathing food while he was overwhelmed, and Clarke finds nothing surprising in an appetite gone with his strength. Henry takes the choice at face value, a man preferring to die obscurely by hunger rather than honourably in battle, then calls it beside the point: a defect of animal spirits might be met with food, but a wounded conscience is out of reach of such succours, dainties being as unwelcome as songs sung to a heavy heart. On the seat he took, Keil and Delitzsch describe a bench along the wall furnished with pillows, Clarke notes that couches were where the ancients sat to eat, and Ellicott identifies the divan running round the walls of Eastern rooms — adding that nothing supports the painters' familiar cave, since the woman seems to have lived in a house of her own at En-dor, with no sign she was in hiding.

The meal gets more attention than its size suggests. Henry observes that the animal was one used in treading out the corn, so could be the worse spared, and reports Josephus applauding her courtesy as a model of compassion where there is no prospect of recompense. Gill adds that such a calf was a dainty dish there, fit for any guest, Josephus describing her as having fed it until it was familiar with her. Clarke explains the speed from the climate: flesh could not be kept long in hot countries, so young animals were kept ready for slaughter and dressed at once; the bread was unleavened because leavening would have taken time there was not, a point Ellicott and Wesley each make in a line. Keil and Delitzsch attribute the kindness to natural sympathy for an unhappy king, rejecting the suggestion that she meant to clear herself of fraud, since she had not deceived him at all. Henry describes the persuasion carefully: the servants and the woman together overbore his resolution not by force but by friendly advice, the only compulsion meant where the parable bids servants compel men to come in, and proof how forcible right words are when they press a man toward his own interest.

The chapter closes with a journey and a verdict. Keil and Delitzsch measure the return to Gilboa at ten miles, covered that night, the battle following next day; and both they and Ellicott quote one judgment on the king: too hardened to grieve for himself or for the predicted fate of his sons and his people, and went in stolid desperation to meet his end — the terrible close of a man the Spirit of God had once turned into another man. Henry has them leave before daylight, to reach the camp and not be seen leaving so scandalous a house, and weighs Josephus again: where Josephus admires a king who would not desert his army though told he would lose life and honour, Henry wonders at a hardness that never turned to repentance and prayer, and suspects that hearing his sons would fall with him reconciled him to his own fall — unlike David, who asked that the hand be against himself and not the people. Clarke ends with numbered articles of his own: that no incantation avails over a departed saint or any disembodied human spirit; that Samuel did appear, sent by the particular mercy of God to warn the king and give him opportunity to make peace with his Maker; and that oracles so circumstantial could come from no demon, the next day's defeat and deaths being knowable to God alone.
